At four. I was told.'"], "setting": "Harrow Point, a small fishing village on a cold northern coast. Late autumn, about three weeks after the equinox. A stone harbour, a tide table nailed to the harbourmaster's door, a lighthouse decommissioned eleven years ago at the end of a black rocky point reached by a causeway path. Now: a little after seven, grey morning, first day after the second night on the causeway. Maren (other coat, dry, knees wet from the quay; no oilskin, no knife) has just followed Dag into the harbour office — smell of diesel and paper, the gauge ticking in its case — and is reading the gauge log open on the desk; Tobias behind her in the doorway. Under last night's readings, in Edvin's small upright hand: 'Pell round the point 4 am. Lines left for the next boat.' Outside: Pell's two whole lines laid carefully on the quay by Aksel, spliced eyes uppermost, his berth water warm; Aksel gone up the slip past the DANGER post (slowed to read Dag's dried bloodied handprint) toward the village, not to the Sandviks' boat; the Sandvik brothers due to go south of the bar today; gulls on the harbour wall, none over the point; causeway head stones bare, sea an hour wrong but ordinary; tower dark. Maren's kitchen: ledger line written, oilskin dripping on the door, two ropes on the stove rail, pool a hand's width from the sill. Britt not yet seen. Seven more nights of the light, then the ninth.", "characters": {"Maren Voss": "woman, 50s, retired harbourmaster, keeps the tide tables by hand in bound ledgers going back decades; widow of Edvin; sleeps badly; wears Edvin's old oilskin with his knife (this morning left it dripping on the door — first time out of it since hop 3 — and went down in her other coat, without the knife); notices small wrongnesses; believes Edvin went to the tower on his ninth night and 'held it'; her hands tied Edvin's hitch unbidden; has understood that 'the rest' is her — her living hand on the outside end — and that she is expected on the ninth night, now eight days off (seven more nights of the light, then the ninth); the bolt turned only when she named Dag harbourmaster — but the same word had no standing over the rope; at the sill she saw in the black water the lamp room from below and a hand on the lamp frame with Edvin's hitch-scar — she knows that hand and has told no one; 'He's asking me to count'; took the knotted tally rope and laid it on the stove rail — the pool drew back to make room; counted seventy-nine stones and told Tobias 'Not yet' (she knows or half-knows what it is); Edvin's knife would not cut the rope; put her own hand on the rope to free Dag — it took her hand gladly and let her go when she opened it: 'Tonight' — she understands it will not always let go, and only releases others when she takes their place; has not told Tobias or Dag what the pull felt like; the lamp went out the instant her boot left the last stone — lit for her walking; told through Dag: eight, and a light each night to count by; said nothing in reply; managing what the village will know (told Britt to bind Dag's hand and let no one see it) — but this morning, when Tobias said Aksel would have it round the village by nine, she said 'Good'; wrote the night's low and flood into the ledger in ink without a source; 'For now'; found the warmth in Pell's berth: 'Just here'; asked Dag 'Told by whom?' and then 'Show me the log' and is now reading Edvin's hand in the gauge log — 'she had read it across a kitchen table for thirty years'. Has not yet spoken about what it says", "Tobias": "Maren's nephew, 19, works the fish counter, skeptical but loyal; his mother (Maren's sister) went south years ago; carries the big torch, a thermos and a spanner (left at the house this morning); quick with figures; knows about the nine days and Edvin's note; identified the cord as this season's rope from Arne's chandlery; offered to hold the rope and was refused as not harbourmaster; heard 'not tonight — the ninth night' and 'eight'; turned the bolt (only after Maren spoke); went first onto the stair; stopped from touching the rope on the step; told Maren to 'Go' with Pell; the dog never once looked at him; counted the knots — nine, one loose; did not see what Maren saw in the water; could not peel Dag's fingers off; 'It let you go' — has seen the rope answers to her hand and nothing else; first through the dip, first off the causeway; watched the pool draw back and said nothing; asked 'Seventy-nine. What is it?' — 'Not yet'; 'It's letting the morning have it'; said he would go to the counter, by the quay first — has not gone; first to notice the warmth in Pell's berth; 'He'll have it round the village by nine' (of Aksel); has followed Maren into the harbour office; has not yet seen the handwriting in the log (knows of it from Dag's account at the plate). Will not let Maren go alone on the ninth night", "Old Pell": "elderly trawlerman, boat moored at the quay, with an old dog that would not bark; saw a man knee-deep at the causeway end at four two nights ago, facing the village, in an oilskin, taken by the rising tide without moving; last night came the wrong way round the point along the dark band and lay alongside the seaward rock on dead water with no line; offered three times to take Maren off, not 'him'; said the water told him two come down and one stays; when the three stepped out he started his engine without a word and backed away along the dark band; his masthead light then went from the seaward dark; this morning his berth is EMPTY — both mooring lines hung slack into the harbour from the rings, whole, eyes spliced, 'never been on anything' (now laid on the quay by Aksel); the harbour water in his berth alone is warm; the gauge log in Edvin's hand says 'Pell round the point 4 am. Lines left for the next boat.'; Dag has given the village version: Pell took his boat out at four, round the point, Sandviks to keep an eye south of the bar; boat, man and dog unaccounted for; possibly 'the one who stays'", "Pell's dog": "old, has never barked; bared its teeth silently at the lit lamp room glass, lay down calm when the first sweep dropped the flood; never once looked at Tobias; gone with the boat", "Dag Halvorsen": "the current harbourmaster, 40ish, Maren's successor, conscientious and a little afraid of her; tall; relies on the printed table and the harbour gauge; put the council's DANGER notice up in the night (white board, red letters, CAUSEWAY UNSAFE / ALL TIDES, his own name under it in a smaller hand); was inside the sealed tower since before Maren arrived; turned the bolt from outside and 'then came in' (unexplained); bought the yellow-flecked rope from Arne on instructions in Edvin's hand in the gauge log; held the inner end and relayed the lamp-carrier's words; came out dry, pale, holding the inner end cut clean. Declared himself the one who 'stays' ('He let me past') — yet came down at once when called; stepped over the knotted rope without looking. On the twenty-sixth stone the rope would not leave his fist until Maren took it from above; across the knuckle of his right hand a raw red rope-burn in the exact place of Edvin's old scar — he has been marked. At the dip: 'It's warm. He said it would be' — 'I don't know who's been saying things to me, Maren.' Read his own notice as if a stranger wrote it; relayed unasked: 'Eight. He says to tell you eight. And that he'll put the light on each night so you can count.' Left a bloodied print in the wet red paint across his own name, which did not run and has dried there. Went home with Britt, docile. THIS MORNING: came to the harbour office at seven in his good jacket, right hand bound in white (Britt did it), carrying the printed tide table to re-pin — going about his duties; said unprompted 'He went round the point. At four. I was told.' Asked by whom: came down at five to read the gauge, found the log open (it was not when he locked up), a line under last night's readings 'not mine' — reported it like a missing fender. Then, seeing Aksel properly, his voice 'changed back into the harbourmaster's' and he gave the plain version: Pell took his boat out at four, round the point, Sandviks keep an eye south of the bar. Held the office door for Maren. Two registers now: the mouthpiece and the official; he can still switch to the official for the village. What he reports to the regional office, whether he has read the whole log page, whether the burn whitens into Edvin's scar — pending", "Aksel": "young deckhand, crews for the Sandvik brothers; came along the quay with a bucket at seven, took Pell's absence for an early start until he drew up the second line and found the spliced eye: 'That's never been on anything.' Heard Dag's 'I was told' and the exchange about the log; was given the official version and said he would tell the Sandviks; laid Pell's line down on the quay very carefully, eye uppermost, and went off without looking back — not to the Sandviks' boat but up the slip, slowing at the DANGER post to read the handprint, and on into the village. Tobias: 'He'll have it round the village by nine.' Maren: 'Good.' The village circle is now opening; what story he tells and to whom first (Arne? the Sandviks? the shop?) pending", "Britt Halvorsen": "Dag's wife; saw the light the first night; last night watched it turn from one until it went out at half past four and came down the slip in a coat over her nightdress; found three soaked people at the DANGER post and the sea where it should not be; saw the handprint; saw water running from Maren's pocket and asked nothing — took Dag home under Maren's instruction to bind the hand and let no one see it; has bound it (white bandage) and apparently let him go to work at five; knows enough to be frightened and has been made a keeper of it; not yet seen this morning", "Arne": "runs the chandlery; got the yellow-flecked rope in this spring; sold it to Dag", "the Sandvik brothers": "fishermen with the berth a yard along from Pell's (water there cold); Aksel crews for them; due to go south of the bar today; Dag has asked, via Aksel, that they keep an eye for Pell", "Edvin Voss": "Maren's late husband, drowned eleven years ago on a night the tide was forty minutes early; the lighthouse went dark the same winter; body never recovered; tied a particular double-looped hitch no one else used; had a small white scar across the knuckle of his right hand from a rope-burn (the 'hitch-scar') — Dag now has a fresh burn in the same place; his knife and oilskin are Maren's now; his ledger note 'nine days — then it holds'; his handwriting — small, upright, leaning nowhere — appeared this spring in Dag's gauge log ('Buy rope. Leave half in the shed. She'll need the rest') and AGAIN last night, under the night's readings: 'Pell round the point 4 am. Lines left for the next boat.' Two nights ago something carrying his old lamp climbed the sealed stair, drew the water down, passed Dag and went up; through Dag it said: not tonight, the ninth night, it only wanted to see whose hand was on the rope; it cut the rope four feet short and left that length on the fourth step with his hitch tied and the loop open; Maren saw, in the water at the sill as if from beneath, the lamp room and his scarred hand turning the lamp; the water gave back the knotted tally rope, now on Maren's stove rail; the plate shut and bolted itself behind the three; his knife would not cut his rope; the rope held Dag until Maren's hand replaced his, then let her go and was hauled back to the tower hand over hand, unhurried; he told Dag the dip would be warm; he put the lamp out the instant Maren stepped off the stones, let the sea back over the path at once, and through Dag told her: eight, and a light each night to count by; this morning the sea gave the causeway head back to the ordinary tide, the warmth appeared in Pell's berth, and he wrote in the log.
